1:
How long after the feast this happened is answered loosely by one and closely by another. John Gill (reformed) offers two possibilities: that the king’s wrath went off with his wine, so that it was a few days at most, or else that the interval covers the expedition of Xerxes into Greece, from which he returned to Shushan in the seventh year of his reign and married Esther that year. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) fixes the limits by dates, the great feast at Susa falling in one year and the setting out for Greece two years later, so that the proposal belongs at some unspecified point between them; the marriage itself, he notes, did not come about until after the return from Greece, the king’s long absence explaining a delay that would otherwise be curious. Both add the same unflattering detail about the interval, Ellicott that even then the king was entangled in more than one illicit connection, and Gill that after the expedition he gave himself up to his amours and on the road to Sardis fell in love with his brother’s wife.

Why the courtiers proposed what they did is given two motives. Gill looks to their own position, that they feared vengeance would be taken on them if Vashti were restored, or at least wished to remove the king’s grief and melancholy. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) put it down to the king’s own change of mind, that when his wrath was appeased he remembered his harsh treatment of Vashti, and the proposal followed. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reports the same from Josephus, that when his anger was over he was exceedingly grieved that the matter had been carried so far, and calls the remedy an extravagant course taken to please the king with another wife instead.

Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) describes without euphemism what was being set up. This was the usual way in which the harem was furnished: the finest women in the land, whether of high or low birth, were sought out and brought in, and they all became the king’s concubines, one only being raised as chief wife to the throne, whose issue was specially entitled to inherit. He notes that the officer named is called the king’s eunuch by the Septuagint and Vulgate and Targum and Syriac alike, since in Eastern countries the women are entrusted to the care of eunuchs only, and he identifies the things for purification as cosmetics, the oil of myrrh and sweet odours named later in the chapter. Ellicott does not soften it either, remarking that the whole verse shows as conclusively as anything could in how degrading an aspect Eastern women were viewed.

On the division of that office the two part slightly. Ellicott makes them separate charges, this eunuch having the virgins while another named later had the custody of the concubines. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) makes him keeper of all the women, both virgins and concubines, who took care of the virgins himself as requiring more caution and committed the concubines to the other as his deputy. Wesley adds a sharp word about the purification, that it was to cleanse them from all impurities and to perfume and adorn and every way prepare them for the king, while for the legal purification of the Jews he never regarded it at all. Henry sets the whole chapter under a frame drawn from two songs, that we have read in the chapter before how God put down one that was high and mighty from her seat and are now to be told how he exalted one of low degree, as the virgin Mary observes in her song and Hannah before her: Vashti being humbled for her height, Esther is advanced for her humility.
5:
Who it was that had been carried away from Jerusalem is a question of grammar with a chronological answer. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) says the antecedent is obviously Kish, though as far as the mere grammar goes it might have been Mordecai, and supports it by arithmetic: the deportation under Nebuchadnezzar fell more than a century before this time, so that the four generations of the pedigree are readily accounted for. John Gill (reformed) reaches the same conclusion from the absurdity of the alternative, that otherwise Mordecai must be a very old man and Esther, his first cousin and the child of his father’s brother, must be at an age one would not reckon among young virgins nor think so amiable — and he reports that according to the former Targum she was seventy-five years old.

What manner of man Mordecai was divides the two who venture on it. Ellicott passes on the identification proposed by Canon Rawlinson with Matacas, the most powerful of the eunuchs in the reign of Xerxes, and argues that Mordecai may be assumed to have been a eunuch himself from the way he is allowed access to the royal harem; he notes also that the name occurs in the lists of those who returned with Zerubbabel. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) gives instead the Targum’s pedigree and the legend attached to it, that this Shimei in the line was the same who cursed David, whom David forbade Joab to kill because he saw in the spirit of prophecy that he was to be the ancestor of Esther and Mordecai, but whom, when he grew old and past having children, David ordered Solomon to put to death.

On her two names they largely agree and then divide. All take Hadassah for a myrtle, Gill adding that Israelites and good men are sometimes compared to it, Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) comparing the Greek women’s names formed from the same plant. For the other name Keil and Delitzsch give an Old Persian word for star with a prosthetic letter, answering to the Greek and to the modern Persian; Clarke calls the name undoubtedly Persian and means a star; Ellicott says it is generally so assumed, and draws a wider inference, that unless the name was given afterwards and used here by anticipation we have an early instance of the common Jewish practice of bearing two names, a Hebrew and a Gentile, as Saul and Paul or John and Mark. Gill allows the Persian sense but offers a Hebrew one first, from a root meaning to hide, because she was hidden in Mordecai’s house. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) settles the order simply, that Hadassah was her name before the marriage and Esther what the king called her after. Clarke adds that she was daughter of Mordecai’s uncle and so his cousin, the Vulgate and Josephus making her his niece, but that it is safest to follow the Hebrew.

Why she pleased the keeper, and why she said nothing of her people, are answered in kind. Gill is careful that it was the chamberlain and not yet the king whom she pleased. Clarke credits the propriety of her deportment and her engaging though unassuming manners, and explains the seven maidens as attendants for the bath and the anointing. Wesley adds a cause the others leave out, the divine power which moves the hearts of men whichever way it pleases. On the concealment Gill makes it lawful rather than prudent, since the question was not asked and she was under no obligation to declare it, being taken for a Persian as one born in Shushan. Clarke makes it prudent and necessary: it was no credit at the Persian court to be a Jew, and had her lineage been known envy might have prevented her ever having access to the king.
12:
Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) offers a reason for the twelve months which he claims no writer he has seen has apprehended. The most beautiful virgins of all the provinces were selected indiscriminately out of every class of the people, so that many of them must have been brought up in low life on coarse and strong food; and it is on that ground, he argues, that so long a course of oil and ointments was needed before they were fit to be presented. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) give the division of the time without comment, six months with oil of myrrh and six with balsam and ointments of purification. John Gill (reformed) explains the order of presentation, that the virgins came in by turns according to the length of time they had been in the house, as he says Herodotus relates of the wives of the Persian kings. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) corrects the single word, that what the version calls the manner of women should be rendered law or ordinance.

What each maiden might take with her sets off what Esther did not take. Clarke explains the provision, that whatever kind of dress or stuff or colour or jewels she thought best to set off her person and render herself more engaging should be given her. Keil and Delitzsch mark the contrast when Esther’s turn came, that she required nothing to take with her but what the keeper of the women appointed. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) takes the permission of ornament or attendance and then adds a defence of her position the others do not attempt: every one whom the king took to his bed was his wife of a lower rank, as Hagar was Abraham’s, so that it would have been no sin nor dishonour to Esther even had she not been made queen.

What became of those not called again is stated plainly and the place disputed. Clarke says the second house was where the concubines were kept, that they went out no more and were never given in marriage to any man, and saw the king’s face no more unless specially called; of the keeper’s name he offers two Persian etymologies, one meaning beardless and the other weak loins, either being a fit epithet for a eunuch, and remarks that names of this kind show at once the reason of their imposition. Gill agrees it was the other apartment of the house of the women, where those the king had made his secondary wives were kept, but reports that Aben Ezra takes the word not of a second house at all but of a second time, and that the Targum renders it again.

The date of the marriage is made to carry an argument. Ellicott places it in the January or February of a particular year, noting that the month named occurs only here and comparing the Egyptian month of similar name, and observes that this must have been very shortly after Xerxes returned to Susa from the West — which accounts for the long delay in replacing Vashti. Clarke gives the month more briefly as answering to part of our December and January. Gill marks the difference between Esther and the rest, that she did not return on the morrow as those who became only concubines did, but was taken to be his wife and designed for his queen, and he notes that Jarchi understood the women she was preferred above to be married women, supposing such were gathered as well as virgins. Clarke describes the crowning in the terms of his own day, that she was made what is now called in the East the Sultana, mistress of all the rest of the wives, who were obliged to pay her the most profound respect.
19:
That the virgins were gathered a second time is read as a comment on the king. John Gill (reformed) rejects the suggestion that the phrase looks back to a collection made when Vashti was chosen, since there is no proof any such collection was then made, and concludes instead that the king’s lust was such that he gathered them again although he already had a queen. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reaches the same judgment from the chronology: the incident cannot be dated precisely, falling somewhere between the marriage and the twelfth year of the reign, but since Esther had been his wife certainly less and possibly much less than five years, the fact of a second gathering shows how the word love is degraded in this connection. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) mark only the function of the passage, that it relates an incident of great importance for the later development of the narrative.

What Mordecai was doing in the gate is settled by an argument from what happens later. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) allows that he may have been one of the king’s officers, the gate being where such men attended to await the royal call, and then rules out the humbler possibility: it is not likely he was the porter, for had he been only that, Haman could have removed him at once. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) agrees he sat there by office, as one of the king’s guards or ministers, and adds that he had been advanced to the place by Esther’s favour. On her continued silence Gill notes that she had not disclosed her kindred since being made queen any more than before, though according to the Targums the king himself urged her to it; Ellicott suggests the verse may be added to meet the supposition that the king would have wished to replace her had he discovered her nation.

Why the two chamberlains conspired is not told, and the gap is filled from elsewhere. Clarke says plainly that we are not informed of their motive, and reports the Targum’s account that they had discovered something concerning Esther; he notes that they were eunuchs. On how the plot came to light he passes on Josephus, that a Jew overheard it and told Mordecai, who told Esther, who told the king in Mordecai’s name, so that Mordecai was registered as the discoverer. Ellicott draws out the consequence, that by this means an increased influence was doubtless gained over the capricious mind of the king, an influence which before long served Esther in good stead.

How the conspirators died is disputed between the two who look into it. Clarke suggests that the words rendered hanged on a tree may rather mean impaled, and describes the manner at length, a pointed stake set upright in the ground and the culprit placed upon its point and drawn down by the legs. Ellicott makes it crucifixion instead, a punishment common among the Persians and especially used on rebels, and cites the crucifying of the dead body of Leonidas by Xerxes’ orders after the desperate stand at Thermopylae. Of the record made of it Ellicott notes only that a sleepless night would afterwards bring the book of the chronicles to be read. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads the whole incident as architecture: the good service is recorded here because mention of it will occur again to Mordecai’s advantage, and though no step is yet taken towards the design of the Jews’ destruction, several steps are already taken towards God’s design of their deliverance, this being one — God giving Mordecai an opportunity of doing the king a good turn beforehand.
